title: He Cannot Deny Himself
subtitle: The one attribute that holds the judgment and the mercy together
teaser: Four lines of an old hymn, and the fourth one breaks the pattern the first three set. Three say: this is what follows from what people do. The fourth says something follows from what God is. Underneath the comfort is the reason nobody escapes Him either — and the two turn out to be the same sentence read from opposite ends.
theme: God's faithfulness rests on His own nature, which is why He can neither call the damage nothing nor let go of the people who did it.

modules.passage: Then the LORD passed in front of Moses and called out: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness,
emphasis: abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness
modules.scriptureContext: Two minutes with the only place in Scripture where God says His own name at length — and what He puts in it.

modules.definition: and faithfulness — truth, reliability, the quality of a thing that holds when it is leaned on
modules.usage: The word closing God's self-description is not a word about feeling. Emet is what a rope has, or fails to have, at the moment weight comes onto it. It runs through the Old Testament 127 times, and its root is the root behind amen. Moses is not told that God is warm. He is told that God is load-bearing.

modules.heading: What God Says When He Says His Own Name
modules.content:
Moses had asked to see God's glory. What he got was a voice going past him, saying a name — and then filling that name in with adjectives.

It is worth noticing what is missing. God does not open with power. He does not open with sovereignty, or holiness, or the ability to unmake what He made. He opens with compassion and grace and patience, and He closes with two words joined so often in Hebrew that they function almost as one: loving devotion and faithfulness. Then, three lines later in the same speech, He adds that He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished.

Both halves are in the name. Neither is a qualification of the other. This is God on the record about Himself, and the record includes the part that comforts and the part that terrifies, spoken in one breath on one mountain.

The second of those two words is emet. It is the plainest of the great Hebrew nouns — not a mood but a property, the thing a floor has when it takes a person's weight without warning. Everything the rest of this week says about God's steadfastness is an unpacking of that one syllable, and everything it says about human unsteadiness is a description of what happens to a people who have that God and keep testing other floors.

modules.prompt: God chose which words went into His own name, and He put reliability in it. Where has a person been asking God to be warm, when what they actually needed was for Him to hold?

modules.heading: A Two-Minute Prayer
modules.prayerText: Lord, You said Your own name out loud so no one would have to guess at You. Let today be the day that name stops being a doctrine and starts being a floor. Amen.

modules.ctaSubtext: That can be the whole of today. Below, when there is time: an old hymn quoted by a man in chains, the verb that turns around inside a single sentence, a fourth-century deacon who framed it as a dilemma God could not escape — and an English poet who spent twenty-seven years certain he had been cast off, writing hymns the whole time.

modules.passage: This is a trustworthy saying: If we died with Him, we will also live with Him; if we endure, we will also reign with Him; if we deny Him, He will also deny us; if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself.
modules.transliteration: arnēsasthai heauton ou dynatai — "to deny Himself He is not able"
emphasis: if we deny Him, He will also deny us
He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself
modules.scriptureContext: Four conditional lines, quoted rather than composed — and the fourth does not do what the first three do.

modules.inlineImageAlt: A vast dark wall with one tall doorway pouring golden light across bare ground, a small figure standing at the edge of the light
modules.inlineImageCaption: The same opening is the way through and the thing being measured against; a person standing at its edge is standing in the light either way.

modules.heading: The Saying He Did Not Write
modules.content:
The letter is written by a man in chains, and by his own account he expects to die in them. He has just told Timothy that the word of God is not bound even though he is. And then he stops writing his own sentences and quotes somebody else's.

"This is a trustworthy saying" is a formula that appears a handful of times in these letters, and it works the way a hymn number works in a service. It signals that what follows is not new. The churches already had these lines. They may have sung them. A man about to be executed reaches for the thing the congregation already knew by heart, which is what people do when they need words that will hold without having to be constructed.

The lines come in four pairs, and three of them run on the same hinge:

If we died with Him, we will also live with Him.
If we endure, we will also reign with Him.
If we deny Him, He will also deny us.

Each one names something on the human side and then names what follows on God's. Death, then life. Endurance, then reigning. Denial, then denial. The logic is symmetrical and it is not difficult, and by the third line a reader knows exactly what shape the fourth one is going to take. Something we do, and then the matching thing He does.

Then the fourth line arrives and refuses the shape.

If we are faithless, He remains faithful.

The symmetry breaks. The mirror stops mirroring. Something is named on the human side — the worst thing yet, worse than the denial in line three by any ordinary reckoning, because faithlessness is not a moment but a condition — and what follows on God's side is not the matching failure. It is the opposite of the matching failure. And then the saying does something no hymn is obliged to do. It explains itself.

For He cannot deny Himself.

Not He will not. Not He has decided not to. The Greek says He is not able. Whoever wrote these four lines understood that the fourth one would be unbelievable without a reason attached, and the reason given is not about His mood toward us at all. It is about what He is.

modules.definition: to deny, disown, refuse to acknowledge a relationship one is being asked about
modules.usage: One verb carries this entire passage, and it appears three times in two verses with the subject changing underneath it. In verse 12 the churches sing ἀρνησόμεθα (arnēsometha), "if we will deny" — and then ἀρνήσεται (arnēsetai), "He will deny." In verse 13 the same verb turns one last time and lands, as an infinitive, on God Himself: ἀρνήσασθαι (arnēsasthai), to deny — with the object no longer a person but Himself, and the whole clause governed by "He is not able."
modules.usageNote: The verb is not a technical or liturgical one. It is the ordinary word for what a man does in a courtyard when he is asked whether he knows someone. ἠρνήσατο (ērnēsato) — "he denied it" — is the exact form Matthew uses of Peter twice in six verses, and John uses twice more. Which means the pivot verse is built out of the most famous failure in the Gospels. The saying is not describing an abstraction. It is describing the courtyard, and then saying that the courtyard did not have the last word.

wordByWord.meaning: to deny — the infinitive under "He is not able" (2 Tim 2:13)
he denied it — Peter, Matthew 26:70 and 26:72

relatedWords.meaning: "faithful" (G4103) and "we are faithless" (G569) are the same root with a negative prefix — so the sentence turns on one word twice: what they stop being, He keeps being
the Hebrew counterpart carried in this morning's opening — God is reliable by nature, which is the Old Testament form of "He cannot deny Himself"

modules.content: Not He will not. The Greek says He is not able.

modules.heading: Two Lines That Will Not Be Harmonized
modules.content:
Verse 12 says that denial is answered with denial. Verse 13 says faithlessness is answered with faithfulness. They sit beside each other, in the same quoted stanza, with nothing between them but a semicolon, and the text makes no attempt to reconcile them.

The commentary tradition has never agreed on what to do about that. One long-standing reading takes verse 13 as pure comfort: human failure cannot cancel a promise God made about Himself, and the last line is the gospel arriving to rescue a stanza that was getting frightening. Another reading, equally old, takes it as warning — God remains faithful to everything He has said, including the sentence directly above it about denial, and a person who reads the fourth line as an escape hatch from the third has misread the word faithful to mean lenient.

Both readings can be defended from the Greek, and the honest position is that the passage will not settle it. What is worth noticing is that even the warning reading gets to the same place about God: whichever way the line points, it points at His consistency rather than at His mood.

And there is a man standing in the middle of this who settles more than the grammar does.

Peter denied Him. Not privately, not ambiguously — three times, out loud, with an oath, and twice in the exact verb this passage is built from. If verse 12 were a rule administered mechanically, the record would end in that courtyard. Instead the same Gospel that records the denial records a charcoal fire on a beach and three questions, and the man who denied Him three times is asked three times whether he loves Him, and then handed a job.

Which rules out one thing with certainty. A denial in a courtyard is not the same as a life lived as denial. Peter is not a loophole in the third line — the text never treats his failure as trivial, and neither does he. He is evidence that the fourth line is doing real work, and that the God being described here distinguishes between a man breaking under pressure and a man who has settled his account and walked.

modules.videoTitle: The Reason You Can Trust God (Even When It Seems Risky)
modules.videoCaption: Five minutes on emet — the Hebrew word behind "faithfulness" in this morning's opening verse, and the Old Testament shape of "He cannot deny Himself."

modules.heading: The Oath and the Signature
modules.ancientTruth: In the ancient world an oath was secured by naming something greater than the one swearing — a god, a king, a city. The guarantee always came from outside and above the person making the promise.
modules.modernApplication: Every serious modern promise still works this way. A signature is backed by a court; a currency by a treasury; a marriage vow by whatever the couple believes stands over them. Reliability is borrowed from something larger.
modules.connectionPoint: Which is why God's promises have a structural problem, and Scripture says so plainly: there is nothing greater for Him to swear by. Hebrews resolves it by saying He swore by Himself, and that the result is two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie.
modules.newTestamentEcho: So the security in 2 Timothy 2:13 is not that God is very determined. It is that the guarantee and the guarantor are the same person, and a person cannot be less than himself.

modules.heading: One Attribute, Facing Two Directions
modules.content:
Around the year 318 a young deacon in Alexandria wrote a short book about why God became human, and in the sixth and seventh sections he framed the whole thing as a problem God could not get out of.

On one side, humanity was rotting, and Athanasius says that letting that stand was not an option — not because God is sentimental but because it "would be unfitting and unworthy of Himself." On the other side, God had said that death would follow. And so, Athanasius writes, "it was unthinkable that God, the Father of Truth, should go back upon His word regarding death in order to ensure our continued existence. He could not falsify Himself; what, then, was God to do?" He even closes the obvious exit: "repentance would not guard the Divine consistency, for, if death did not hold dominion over men, God would still remain untrue."

That is 2 Timothy 2:13 with the machinery exposed. The reason God cannot walk away from people who have broken faith with Him is the same reason He cannot pretend the breaking did not happen. Both would require Him to be untrue to Himself, and untruth is the one thing the name in Exodus 34 rules out.

Anselm, writing around 1098, works the same ground from the other end. Suppose sin were simply passed over. Then, he says, "with God there will be no difference between the guilty and the not guilty; and this is unbecoming to God." A deity who overlooks everything has not become kinder. He has become unable to tell people apart, which is not mercy but blindness — and blindness is a defect, and defects cannot be attributed to God.

So the accountability and the mercy are not two attributes in tension, with God choosing between them case by case. Tozer put the objection down flatly: "The familiar picture of God as often torn between His justice and His mercy is altogether false to the facts." It is one attribute facing two directions. He will not call the damage nothing, because that would be a lie. He will not abandon what He swore, because that would also be a lie.

Which leaves exactly one place for this to go, and Paul names it in Romans: God put Christ forward publicly, and He did it "so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus." The cross is not God being talked out of judgment by His own affection. It is God being consistent with Himself at His own expense — the only place in the universe where the two directions of that one attribute meet, and the meeting costs Him rather than us.

There is a place where this consistency looks almost unbearable from the inside. Numbers says God is not a man, that He should lie, "neither the son of man, that he should repent" — the verb is וְיִתְנֶחָ֑ם (veyitnecham), from the root that means to relent or change one's mind. Centuries later, Hosea has God saying of the people He is about to hand over: "mine heart is turned within me, my repentings are kindled together." That word — נִחוּמָֽי (nichumay), my relentings — is built from the very same root, and it occurs only three times in the entire Old Testament.

So the God who does not relent describes His own insides as relentings, kindled. Neither text is embarrassed by the other. Scripture is not offering a God so consistent that nothing moves in Him; it is offering a God whose consistency is not the absence of that movement but the reason the movement can be trusted.

modules.heading: The Man Who Believed He Had Been Cast Off
modules.content:
William Cowper wanted a quiet job. The clerkship of the journals of the House of Lords was transacted in private, and a man who dreaded any public exhibition of himself could survive it. He admitted later, in writing, that he and a friend had discussed the post and "both expressed an earnest wish for his death" — the death of the man who held it — and that he had therefore coveted what God had commanded him not to covet, "in the spirit of a murderer."

The man died. Then a parliamentary dispute meant Cowper would have to appear at the bar of the House to claim the place. He prepared for months, and when the day came he could not do it. In the collapse that followed he tried more than once to end his life. He gives the date himself: from the 7th of December 1763, a conviction of sin and expectation of instant judgment did not leave him until the middle of July following. He was taken to St Albans, into the care of Dr Nathaniel Cotton.

The turn came in a chair by a window. He picked up a Bible and, in his account, "the first verse I saw was the 25th of the 3rd of Romans" — the propitiation through faith in His blood. He wrote that he received strength to believe it, and that he thought he should have died of gratitude and joy.

He had eight years. Then in January 1773 the darkness came back, and this time it stayed, carrying with it a fixed conviction that he personally had been cast off by God. He held that conviction for twenty-seven years, until he died.

And he went on writing hymns the entire time.
modules.connectionToTheme: Cowper is the fourth line of the stanza with a face. His own faithfulness collapsed and did not recover; his sense of being held vanished and never came back. What the passage claims is not that his feelings were unreliable and God's promise steadied them. It is that the promise was not resting on his feelings in the first place — which is the only version of this doctrine that is any use to a person in his condition.

modules.heading: Never Differs From Himself
modules.content: Tozer reduced the whole matter to a sentence with nothing left over: "To say that God is immutable is to say that He never differs from Himself."
modules.historicalContext: From The Knowledge of the Holy (1961), chapter 9. Tozer wrote the book as a corrective — his conviction was that low thinking about God was the church's central disease, and that the cure was not enthusiasm but accuracy.

modules.heading: What It Costs Each of Two Readers
modules.content:
This doctrine is usually filed under comfort, and for one kind of reader that filing is correct. Someone who has broken the same promise to God enough times to have quietly concluded He must be finished with them is being told something specific: the thing holding the arrangement together was never their consistency, so their inconsistency has not dissolved it. Cowper's twenty-seven years are the extreme test of that sentence, and the sentence survives them.

But the same doctrine costs a second reader something, and it is worth being honest about the size of the bill.

Someone who is managing — competent, self-directed, treating God as a resource to be consulted rather than a Lord to be answered — usually assumes that if God is that committed, the matter is more or less closed. Athanasius blocks that exit before it opens. The consistency that will not let go is the same consistency that will not pretend. A God who never differs from Himself is not a God who eventually stops noticing.

What that rules out is a specific and very common arrangement: treating divine faithfulness as permission. The stanza itself forecloses it, because verse 12 is still sitting there in the same breath as verse 13 and the passage declines to remove it.

And six verses later the letter puts both halves on one object. It describes a foundation with a seal cut into it, and the seal has two lines: "The Lord knows those who are His," and, "Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord must turn away from iniquity." One seal. Two sentences. The security and the summons stamped into the same stone, which is what has been true since the mountain in Exodus, where the name that abounds in loving devotion also declines to leave the guilty unpunished.

modules.passage: For my name’s sake will I defer mine anger, and for my praise will I refrain for thee, that I cut thee not off. Behold, I have refined thee, but not with silver; I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction. For mine own sake, even for mine own sake, will I do it: for how should my name be polluted? and I will not give my glory unto another.
emphasis: For mine own sake, even for mine own sake, will I do it
modules.scriptureContext: The prophets got here first. God gives His reason for not cutting the people off, and the reason He gives is Himself — said twice, in case once could be mistaken for a figure of speech.

modules.prompt: The passage sets a warning and a rescue side by side and refuses to remove either one. Which of the two has a person been quietly deleting?
additionalQuestions: If God's commitment does not rest on a person's performance, what does that change about the last thing they did badly — and what does it fail to change?
Cowper never got his assurance back and kept writing anyway. What would it look like to keep going without the feeling that usually justifies going on?
"For mine own sake, even for mine own sake." Where would it be a relief, rather than an insult, to be loved for reasons that have nothing to do with oneself?

modules.heading: A Practice for Today
modules.instruction: This one is done standing, and it takes about two minutes. The point is to feel the difference between holding and being held.

steps.title: Grip
steps.description: Stand and close both hands hard, arms down at the sides. Hold it. Name silently the things currently being held together by effort — the promise being kept by willpower, the reputation, the version of yourself that has to stay up.

steps.title: Open
steps.description: Let both hands fall open, palms up, and leave them open longer than is comfortable. Say once, quietly: He cannot deny Himself.

steps.title: Stand
steps.description: Stay standing with the hands open and do nothing else for one slow minute. Notice that nothing fell. That is the whole exercise.

modules.heading: The Floor Under the Floor
modules.content:
The stanza began with four conditional lines and a symmetry that broke on the last one. It is worth returning to why it broke.

Three lines describe a world where outcomes follow from what people do, and that world is real. Scripture never pretends otherwise, and the rest of this week is largely about it — the field a person plants, the road a person walks, the covenant a person breaks.

The fourth line does not deny that world. It says there is something underneath it.

Moses was given a name on a mountain and the name ended in reliability. Isaiah was given a reason and the reason was God's own. A young deacon in Alexandria worked out that mercy and judgment were the same fact seen from two sides. A dying man in a Roman prison quoted a hymn his churches already knew. And an English poet who spent twenty-seven years certain he had been cast off wrote, in a letter to his friend, "There is a mystery in my destruction, and in time it shall be explained."

He did not get the explanation. He got the mystery, and kept writing.

What this passage offers is not a feeling of security and not a guarantee that the feeling will come. It offers a floor, and it says the floor is God's own consistency rather than anyone's grip on it. Cowper's hands came open and stayed open for twenty-seven years, and he did not fall through.

A person can spend a whole life trying to be steady enough to deserve a steady God. The stanza in this letter says the steadiness was never the entry requirement. It was the thing that was already there, holding the floor up, on the days it was noticed and on the very many days it was not.

modules.heading: Closing Prayer
modules.prayerText: Father, You said Your own name out loud on a mountain, and You put both halves in it — the devotion that will not let go and the truth that will not pretend. Forgive us for wanting only one of them. Where we have used Your faithfulness as permission, take the permission away. Where we have decided You are finished with us, be more stubborn than our decision. We do not ask to feel held today; we ask to be held today, and to keep walking whether or not the feeling ever comes back. You cannot deny Yourself. Be, this day, exactly what You said You were. Amen.
modules.breathPrayer: Breathing in: You cannot deny Yourself. Breathing out: so I do not have to hold this up.

modules.heading: Today's Commitment
modules.commitment: I will stop treating my consistency as the thing holding my life with God together, and I will stop treating His consistency as permission.
leavingAtCross: The private verdict that God has quietly written me off
The arrangement where His faithfulness excuses my drift
The grip I have kept on things I was never holding up
receivingFromCross: A name spoken aloud by God about Himself, with both halves in it
A promise whose guarantor and guarantee are the same person
Room to keep walking on a day when nothing about it feels true

modules.heading: One Question
modules.question: Why does the saying add "for He cannot deny Himself" to the end of the fourth line?
options: To soften the warning in the line above it
To ground God's faithfulness in His own nature rather than in anything human — which is why it holds when ours fails, and why it never becomes permission
To promise that a believer's faith will never actually fail
To indicate that God overlooks sin
modules.explanation: The clause supplies a reason, and the reason is about God rather than about us. Because His faithfulness rests on His own consistency, it survives human failure — and for the same reason it cannot be turned into an allowance, since a God who never differs from Himself is also a God who never stops telling the truth about what has happened.

modules.heading: The Voice Behind Today
modules.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
modules.bio: A deacon, later bishop of Alexandria, who wrote On the Incarnation while still a young man — around 318, before the Council of Nicaea. He spent roughly seventeen years of his episcopate in exile, banished five separate times under four emperors for refusing to soften what he believed about Christ's divinity.
modules.keyQuote: He could not falsify Himself; what, then, was God to do?
modules.lessonForUs: The framing of this passage as a dilemma — God unable to abandon and unable to pretend, both for the same reason — is seventeen centuries old. It was not invented to comfort anyone. It was worked out by a man who kept being exiled for insisting that God is exactly who He says He is.

modules.videoCaption: A thirty-minute go-deeper for later in the day: the tension between the unconditional and conditional strands of covenant blessing, and where it is resolved.

modules.heading: Sources & Further Study

relatedScriptures.text: God's self-naming in full. Verse 7 carries the other half — "Yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished" — in the same speech as the loving devotion.
The two texts quoted in today's pivot. Numbers: God does not repent. Hosea: "my repentings are kindled together." Same Hebrew root, opposite directions, held without embarrassment.
Where the two directions of the one attribute meet — "so as to be just and to justify."
Six verses on: one seal, two lines. The security and the summons cut into the same stone.
The oath problem and its solution: God swore by Himself, because there was no one greater.

resources.title: Athanasius, On the Incarnation, §§6-7

(Sister Penelope Lawson), Geoffrey Bles / Centenary Press, London, 1944 — the edition C. S. Lewis introduced. Free at ccel.org. The scholarly alternative is Archibald Robertson's NPNF translation, which renders the same argument in sterner English.

resources.title: Anselm, Cur Deus Homo, Book I, ch. XII
resources.description: "There is also another thing which follows if sin be passed by unpunished…" — quoted verbatim from Sidney Norton Deane's translation, St. Anselm: Basic Works, Open Court, 1903.

resources.title: A. W. Tozer, The Knowledge of the Holy (1961), chs. 9 and 15
resources.description: Source of "He never differs from Himself" (ch. 9) and "The familiar picture of God as often torn between His justice and His mercy is altogether false to the facts" (ch. 15).

resources.title: C. H. Spurgeon, sermon no. 1453, "Eternal Faithfulness Unaffected by Human Unbelief," Metropolitan Tabernacle Pulpit vol. 25 (1879)
resources.description: Spurgeon's own sermon on 2 Timothy 2:13, where he lists the three things God cannot do — die, lie, and be deceived — and calls them not limits on His power but the magnifying of His majesty. Note that the SpurgeonGems edition modernizes spelling and capitalizes deity pronouns; the 1879 setting does not.

resources.title: William Cowper, Memoir of the Early Life of William Cowper, Esq., Written by Himself
resources.description: Source of today's story and of every quoted phrase in it, including the coveting "in the spirit of a murderer," the dating of the darkness from 7 December 1763, and Romans 3:25 in the chair by the window. Published in 1816 against Cowper's express wishes, and printed editions are edited; the scholarly text is King & Ryskamp, The Letters and Prose Writings of William Cowper (Oxford, 1979-86). The letter quoted at the close — "There is a mystery in my destruction" — is to John Newton, 13 January 1784. A widely repeated story that Cowper wrote "God Moves in a Mysterious Way" on the night of a suicide attempt is not true: the manuscript evidence places the hymn before the 1773 collapse, and Samuel Greatheed, who preached Cowper's funeral three weeks after his death, said it was composed on a solitary walk in the fields in presentiment of the illness to come.

resources.title: Greek and Hebrew data
resources.description: arneomai (G720) — 33 NT occurrences, 4 in 2 Timothy; the three forms in 2:12-13 are arnēsometha (future middle 1pl), arnēsetai (future middle 3sg) and arnēsasthai (aorist middle infinitive), and ērnēsato at Matthew 26:70, 72 is the same verb used of Peter. pistos (G4103) and apistoumen (G569) share the root pist-. emet (H571), 127 OT occurrences, root aman. veyitnecham (H5162, Hitpael) at Numbers 23:19; nichumay (H5150, from H5162) at Hosea 11:8 — 3 OT occurrences total. Note on Isaiah 48:11: the verb "will I do it" is present in the Hebrew; the ellipsis some commentators mark is the word "name."

modules.forDeeperStudy: Read Exodus 34:1-9, then Numbers 23:19 beside Hosea 11:8-9, then 2 Timothy 2:8-19 in one sitting. The question to carry through all three: in each passage, what is God said to be unable to do — and who benefits from the inability?
